title: Jeremiah 41:11–18
context: Jeremiah 41:11–18 is told by the narrator. Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains hear of Ishmael’s deeds, pursue him, and find him by the great waters in Gibeon (41:11–12; compare 2 Samuel 2:13, “by the pool of Gibeon”, named without identifying the two). The captives turn back to Johanan with gladness, but Ishmael escapes with eight men to the Ammonites (41:13–15). Johanan and the captains take the rescued remnant, men of war, women, children, and eunuchs, and go to Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt because they fear the Chaldeans after the murder of the governor Babylon had appointed (41:16–18). The place name Geruth Chimham is of uncertain meaning, perhaps a lodging place, and some connect Chimham with the Chimham who went with David in 2 Samuel 19:37–38, though the link is not certain. The planned flight leads into chapters 42–43, where the remnant asks Jeremiah to pray for guidance and then goes to Egypt against the word he brings (42:1–3; 43:7). The parallel in 2 Kings 25:26 says briefly that the people and captains went to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans; the accounts are named without harmonizing. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: fear, grief, and the search for safety mark the remnant, and the question of whether they will listen to the LORD’s word comes next.

verses.text: But when Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan the son of Kareah and the captains heard of all the evil Ishmael had done. Arminian readers note that Johanan, who had warned Gedaliah (40:13–16), now acts to rescue the captives, and they see a leader responding to injustice with resolve and courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link with Johanan’s earlier warning and observe that his concern for the remnant is consistent. They read the verse as turning the account from tragedy toward rescue, while noting that the narrator does not yet evaluate Johanan’s leadership.

verses.text: then they took all the men, and went to fight with Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and found him by the great waters that are in Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes: They went to fight with Ishmael and found him by the great waters in Gibeon. Arminian readers note that Gibeon lay north of Jerusalem, and some connect the great waters with the pool of Gibeon in 2 Samuel 2:13, named without identifying the two with certainty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification of the great waters loosely. They read the verse as showing that Ishmael’s flight toward the Ammonites was interrupted, and they observe that the narrator’s interest lies in the rescue of the captives rather than in the details of the place.

verses.text: Now when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, then they were glad.
verses.arminianNotes: When the people with Ishmael saw Johanan and the captains, they were glad. Arminian readers note the joy of the captives at the sight of rescue, and they see in it a small reversal amid many sorrows, as people taken by force find a way back to freedom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same joy and read the verse as a moment of relief in a grim account. They observe that the captives’ gladness shows they had been taken against their will, and both traditions see in it a picture of rescue that the remnant greatly needed.

verses.text: So all the people who Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned about and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
verses.arminianNotes: All the people Ishmael had carried captive from Mizpah turned about and went back to Johanan. Arminian readers note that the captives were freed without battle, and they see the remnant rescued from a fate that seemed certain only moments before, a mercy in a dark time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the turning of the captives happens quickly, and they read it as a deliverance within the narrative. They observe that the narrator records the rescue simply and without attributing it to any particular means beyond the arrival of Johanan and his men.

verses.text: But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites. Arminian readers note that Ishmael escapes justice, at least for now, and they observe that he arrived with ten men (41:1) and leaves with eight, though the text does not explain the difference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same detail and do not speculate about the missing men. They read Ishmael’s escape as leaving the remnant exposed to Babylon’s anger over Gedaliah’s murder, which shapes the fear that drives the decisions of the following verses.

verses.text: Then Johanan the son of Kareah and all the captains of the forces who were with him took all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, from Mizpah, after he had killed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam—the men of war, with the women, the children, and the eunuchs, whom he had brought back from Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan and the captains took all the remnant they had recovered from Ishmael, the men of war, women, children, and eunuchs. Arminian readers note that Johanan now becomes the leader of the remnant, and they see the responsibility that falls on him for the fragile community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same shift in leadership and read the list of people as showing the vulnerability of the remnant. They observe that the narrator’s careful listing reflects the importance of these survivors for the story that continues in chapters 42–44.

verses.text: They departed and lived in Geruth Chimham, which is by Bethlehem, to go to enter into Egypt
verses.arminianNotes: They departed and lived in Geruth Chimham, by Bethlehem, intending to go to Egypt. Arminian readers note that the place name is uncertain, perhaps a lodging place, and that some connect Chimham with the Chimham of 2 Samuel 19:37–38, though the link is not certain and is named without pressing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification loosely. They note that the intention to go to Egypt leads into chapters 42–43, where the remnant asks Jeremiah for the LORD’s guidance (42:1–3) and then goes to Egypt against his word (43:7), named here without harmonizing.

verses.text: because of the Chaldeans; for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had killed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor over the land.
verses.arminianNotes: They went because of the Chaldeans, for they were afraid of them after Ishmael had killed the governor Babylon had appointed. Arminian readers note that fear drives the remnant’s plans, and they see the danger of making decisions out of fear before seeking the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same fear and observe that 2 Kings 25:26 reports the flight to Egypt briefly, named without harmonizing. They read the verse as setting up the question of chapter 42, whether the remnant will trust the LORD’s word or their own plans.
